It will require a joint effort on behalf of the federal, provincial and municipal Governments, and it will require fundamental changes-
So you're writing young people off.
-which we are in the process of engaging in.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Questions and comments are now terminated. On debate with the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis).

Mr. Speaker, I must say at the outset that I was somewhat disappointed when the Minister of State for Youth (Mr. Charest) had virtually nothing to say when the question was put to him with respect to the extremely high levels of youth unemployment in Vancouver, British Columbia, and right across the country. The fact is that when one looks at the Budget one notices that there is not a single mention of what the Government plans to do, or is even thinking of doing, to assist young people who are out of work. I assumed that when the Minister of State for Youth rose in his place to participate in this debate he would have outlined many of the programs he was planning to introduce. Having taken that opportunity one can only assume that he has no plans. We can assume that the Government is prepared to let young people hang out to dry, ignoring the plight which they face. I find that completely unacceptable. Quite frankly, I do not find many things in the Budget which are acceptable. I do not say that there is nothing good in it at all. I will come to the good parts in the last two or three seconds of my presentation.
I wish to comment on what I feel are the very serious shortcomings of the 1987 Budget. There is an old adage that says that if one cannot stand the heat then one must get out of the kitchen. I guess that is what the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) felt when, the day after the Budget, he jumped into a plane and headed for West Palm Beach. He is getting out of the country. Just like the time when the heat came on with all the scandals and he slipped away out of the country.
He is not here during what has to be a critical debate. When he promised to stand in the House and make a statement on South Africa he has not made one. He has not made a statement on South Africa yet. I believe that he will not make a statement on South Africa. I ask Hon. Members to wait and see. Again, we have had promises and promises but when the heat comes on, out he goes out of the country.
I ask Hon. Members to cast their minds back to when the Minister for International Trade (Miss Carney) was negotiating what is probably the most important agreement that Canada will negotiate in this decade regarding the forest industry. She was holidaying on the beaches of Maui. She could not even be here for the final critical and crucial
negotiations. That is the kind of Government we have. When Members of it cannot stand the heat then they get out of the kitchen. Not only do they get out of the kitchen, they get out of the house-they get out of the country. I suspect for a great many Canadians the polls indicate that they would just as soon that the Prime Minister stayed out of the country. I believe 22 per cent is the last official barometer reading with respect to the number of people in Canada who, when the question was put with respect to whether or not they would support the Government, said yes. The other 78 per cent said no. That is a pretty damaging comment when one considers that it comes just two-and-a-half years after the public gave the Government the largest mandate ever given a Government in Canadian history.
The Prime Minister explained why the people of Canada are feeling as they are. A few days ago on February 11, 1987, the Prime Minister said:
These are difficult moments, obviously. We will be judged by the manner in which we responded.
That is exactly what is going on. The people of Canada are judging this Government on the way it is responding to some very critical economic problems that are facing Canada.
When I listened to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) delivering his Budget Speech, I was left deadened by the impact. There was nothing in it. As some people said, it was a "do nothing" Budget. We were expecting some leadership, direction and initiative by the Government during difficult economic times, and there is none of this in the Budget. The Minister of Finance could have issued a short press release, put it in the mail, and announced the two or three tax increases that will affect every Canadian, and that would be it.
However, in looking at the Budget, an appropriate term to call it would be a "fudge-it" Budget. There is a great deal of fudging going on today. For example, the Government states that unemployment is coming down. The Minister of Finance has said dozens of times in the last few hours that unemployment decreased last year. Technically that is true, because a year ago today the unemployment rate was 9.8 per cent. Now it is now 9.7 per cent. So over 12 months the unemployment rate has decreased one-tenth of 1 per cent. Surely to goodness that is nothing to brag about. As a matter of fact, I would expect the Minister of Finance to be embarrassed for suggesting that they have been successful as a Government and have brought down unemployment. I am certain there is no person in the House who would say that decreasing unemployment one-tenth of 1 per cent over 12 months is appropriate, and is at all acceptable. We are led to believe that unemployment is coming down. Well, it is, but by an infinitesimal amount.
When we listened to the Minister of Finance talk about economic growth, we heard him state that it is on course and on target. What course is it? What target is it that the Government is looking at? When I look at the figures put out
February 20, 1987

by Statistics Canada, I find that the growth rate in 1984 was 5.5 per cent when the Government took over the administration. In 1985, it dropped to 4 per cent. In 1986, it dropped to 3.3 per cent. The Minister of Finance projects that in 1987 it will be 2.8 per cent. In other words, while the Conservative Government has been in power, the growth rate has been dropping year after year, and the Minister of Finance predicts it will drop again this year. He states that they are on target, that the growth rates are what they have been working towards. One assumes that they must be improving, but the facts are that the growth rates are declining year after year.
I could go on in terms of this "fudge-it" Budget. In the last Budget the Minister of Finance predicted that the deficit for last year would be $29.5 billion. In the Budget the other day the Minister of Finance said that it was not $29.5 billion, it was $32 billion. In other words, the Minister of Finance did not come close to what he projected 12 months ago. The assumption in the country is that the deficit is going down year after year. The Minister of Finance's projections were out by $2.5 billion.
If the Government is on course, its programs are on course and its strategy is on course, then it begs the question, on course for whom? Who is benefiting from this course that the Government is on? In looking at who is paying for what, it will be noticed that since the Conservative Government has taken power, corporations have actually paid $2 billion less. In other words, corporation taxes collectively have gone down. The corporate sector has done and is doing extremely well when it comes to taxes. But when you look at people and personal taxes, the situation is dramatically reversed. While corporations have had a $2 billion drop in taxes over the life of this administration, people have paid an extra $22.8 billion in increased personal taxes. That is a serious increase, which averages out to $2,000 for every man, woman and child in Canada. That is incredible. I do not expect that there is a time in Canadian history that over a two-and-a-half-year period the federal Government has managed to drop corporate taxes and increase personal taxes so much. It has been accomplished by the Government.
We heard earlier in today's debate that the slogan now will be, "Make the kids pay". Make the kids pay additional taxes. Widen the tax base to include the snack foods that young people tend to buy, and raise an extra $60 million year after year. On top of that, we have seen the sales tax increase once, twice, three times. When the Conservative Government took over power, the sales tax across Canada was 9 per cent. Today it is 12 per cent. That is an increase of 3 per cent in less than three years. It is not only an increase one, two, three times, but it is also a broadening of the tax base to include all types of things that hitherto had not been federally taxed. As a result of this most recent Budget we now include snack foods that young children tend to use.
In terms of the "fudge-it" Budget the assumption is that there is some equality in the Government's programs. But when you look at the facts as they are applied to our tax
The Budget-Mr. Riis
system and the taxes that have been levied by the Government, you find that they are extremely discriminatory against people and in favour of corporations. They favour upper income earners and are against low and middle income earners.
When the Prime Minister was speaking in Quebec before the Budget, he mentioned that money for regional economic development will be very thin. I am afraid that he was wrong. Money for regional economic development is non-existent and has been reduced. The question that must be asked is, have the Minister of Finance and the economic Ministers in the Government travelled around Canada? Have they been outside of Metropolitan Toronto?
Yes.
Have they been out to northern Alberta?
Yes.
Have they been out to British Columbia?
Yes.

Have they been to Atlantic Canada, and visited parts of Newfoundland where the unemployment rates are 35 per cent? Have they visited central British Columbia where the unemployment rates are close to 25 per cent? If they have, why did they not do something about it? Why do they accept the human tragedy that is unfolding as a result of the extremely dramatic high levels of unemployment in the regions of Canada?
What I think has to be the most alarming, shocking, astounding figure that I have read in the last number of weeks is regarding the number of real jobs that were created in Canada in 1986. The net number of jobs created in Canada in 1986 was 137,000. To some people 137,000 new jobs is a reasonably impressive record. The critical point is that out of those 137,000 new jobs created in 1986, 132,000 were created in Ontario. In other words, 96 per cent of the new jobs created in this great country were created in one single province. They were not even equally spread out in that province. The lion's share of those jobs occurred in Metropolitan Toronto and the surrounding area. They were by and large tied to the automotive industry which the Government is now failing to support. That is an incredible statistic.
When the Government talks about the jobs that are being created, when it talks about its success at job creation, does it mention to the representatives from the Northwest Territories, western Canada, Atlantic Canada, northern Ontario, and Quebec where those jobs were created? Do they explain to Canadians that virtually all the jobs created last year were created in a very small portion of Canada, mainly in the greater Toronto area? Yet people talk about the initiatives that this Government is taking in regional economic development.

For most Canadians the situation has actually worsened. There are 1,342,000 people who are officially recognized as being unemployed, men, women and young people in search of work. At this rate, if we were going to accept it as the approach to fighting unemployment, we would have to wait 270 years before we actually obtained full employment.
The unemployed and under-employed across Canada were certainly not impressed with this Budget. I cannot find a single thing in the Budget that will result in a single job being created anywhere in Canada. I can find a number of areas that will likely result in job loss. When you add more taxes on gasoline, diesel and aviation fuel, on airline travel, on food that people purchase on a weekly basis, on alcohol and tobacco, we have calculated that all this would amount to about $70 a family each year in additional taxes. And that results in job loss. It means that $60 million in the snack food list alone will not be there for circulation in the economy.
We are very concerned that the Minister of Finance did not see it appropriate to even mention the word poverty in his Budget Speech. There are four million people in poverty, which is a tragic figure-
One in every five children.

The Hon. Member for Vancouver indicates that one in every five children lives below the poverty line, not at the poverty line but below it. While the Government spends days and days and weeks and weeks talking about banking centres, the food banks
continue in the major cities and smaller communities across Canada. Thousands and thousands of men and women in 1987 have to line up to obtain a package of food to take home for their families.

This is why some of us felt that we were betrayed as Canadians by the lack of action in this Budget. I have not had a chance to say much about what I call the abandonment of the family farm and ranch. There were no provisions to ensure that long-term low-interest money was made available to the family farm and ranch across Canada. Again, I did not hear anything about any special western or eastern development fund. I remember hearing from the Liberals about the famous Western Development Corporation that never saw the light of day.
In summary, all the Minister of Finance has promised us, after promising it to us in 1984, 1985, 1986 and now in 1987, is that he will eventually get to tax reform in whatever form that might take. In closing let me say that it is time we had a Government that put full employment at the top of its agenda as its goal and introduced strategies in the regions right across Canada to ensure that every man and woman would have an opportunity to be fully and meaningfully employed at a job that would contribute to the benefits of Canada, see Canada grow and ensure that our sons, daughters, grandsons and granddaughters will have the same opportunity.

Mr. Speaker, I think it is well understood that I am the last speaker in the debate before our recess next week. I want to speak to the many people across the country who are asking parliamentarians what is going on. I do not intend to get into this high school debate over numbers. It does not explain anything to them at all. I want to put down, in terms most of us can understand, what is going on, not only in our country but in many others as well.
There is no question that many countries of the world in the early 1970s proceeded on a course which we can only describe now as a mess. In Canada the mess started by 1972 and corresponded to the high increase in metal prices that year and oil prices in 1972 to 1973. Not only our country but all countries seemed to go mad trying to spend more money. Every time there was a problem, money was thrown at it. As a
The Budget-Mr. Hamilton
result, we have the situation we are in now. I do not see any way where people of intellectual honesty and integrity can see an end to it for at least 10 years. Even then there will still be remnants. If you think we are in serious trouble, take a look at the country to the south of us and the horrible mess they are in in Europe.
It is passing strange, is it not, given that all these industrialized countries were so strong a few years ago, that little Canada happens to be leading the slow race back towards recovery? That is because this Government, knowing it could not solve all problems, quickly stated its intentions in a statement in this House in November, 1984, of moving slowly to get at these problems, with consultation and all the rest of it. No one wants to pretend that we are racing ahead to a great future. All we are doing is clawing and scratching to stop the mess from continuing. From now on I hope it will turn slowly and will begin to go down.
This debate has been going on among the intellectuals of the world for the last 40 years, but it has not moved into the legislatures of the world. In the western world in the last 50 years we have believed in a religion known as the Keynesian consensus. That is the consensus that in order to get a country going you simply pour more money out. It is associated with a lot of other theories, including monetarism. I ask my colleagues in the House to put their minds, for the time that we are in our positions as Members of Parliament, to trying to improve on what we have been doing for the last 30 or 40 years through the lessons of the past.
I am going to take two or three facts and develop them a little bit. In 1961, a young President of the United States was facing a deficit in the Budget of the United States and was persuaded not to raise taxes, which was the orthodox way of balancing the Budget, but to reduce them on the things people needed. He took that advice in 1961, but we did not know the result until about 1963. His Budget reduced taxes by about $10 billion in the United States. That was a lot of money in those days. As a result, there was a surplus of $10 billion at the end of the two-year period. Kennedy did not live much longer than 1963, but the new President saw the evidence that by reducing taxes they got more money and were able to do all the things people wanted and to fight the war in Vietnam as well.
In the Reagan Budget of 1981, 20 years later, he too reduced taxes and got more money back in. As you know, the Americans went on spending. The Budget of 1979 in Canada, which we refer to as the Crosbie Budget, won world acclaim among thinkers, but was laughed and voted out of this House by the Liberal-NDP alliance. I know there were Members in both the Liberal and the New Democratic Parties who tried to stop that madness. They wanted to defeat the Government on this issue which they had laughed at, and the Liberal Party destroyed itself. When they went to the country they won the election and had to face their own mess. The Liberal-NDP

February 20, 1987
The Budget-Mr. Hamilton
alliance of that period, with its policy of spend, spend, spend, created the mess which we have in Canada today.
There are people who are trying to see their way through the mist. One different philosophy comes from a Canadian by the name of Mundell. I have mentioned this in the House before and will refer to it again. Long after the Crosbie Budget was defeated a magazine called The Public Interest described that Budget as the dissolution of the Keynesian consensus. The article was written by James W. Dean, another Canadian from British Columbia. He said:
On December 13, 1979, the government of Canada fell. For just six months the Conservatives had governed with a parliamentary minority, and they were defeated on a vote of no confidence. The issue was their first budget-a budget that rejected Keynesian economic policies, replacing them with radically different recommendations. Unemployment and slow growth were to be fought not by increasing the federal deficit but by reducing it.
I think that is enough of the facts. There were people in 1979 and 1980 who saw through the mist that one government in the world had learned a little from the experiences of Kennedy and from what Mundell was preaching.
What is this theory? I am not going to go into it in great detail. I am going to quote one of the editorial writers for The Wall Street Journal in 1982. Judy Steed, a Canadian reporter, or pundit if you want to call her that, described Mundell in The Globe and Mail of Saturday, April 24, 1982. I hope you will listen to this rather exaggerated judgment. She said:
The Mundellian thesis, according to Mr. Wanniski-
-he was the editor of The Wall Street Journal at that time-
-is "truly revolutionary." It upsets the monetarist and Keynesian models that have vied for supremacy among economists for the past 40 years. In the world according to Keynes, government intervenes in the marketplace, spreading money around (through taxation and services) to make sure buyers can spend. Consumer demand is what counts.
Mr. Mundell turns the demand model inside out. Supply creates demand, he argues. "A necessary condition for employment is that you have a sufficient number of employers. But if you tax employers excessively, you won't have much employment." Hence taxes must be cut to give producers sufficient incentives to create more supply.
That, in a paragraph, gives one part of the Mundell hypothesis. I repeat that this Budget is not out of harmony with what the Minister did in 1979. The only trouble was that we did not know he had done it. It is not out of harmony with the statement of 1984. I think that members of all Parties and Canadians who love their country should admire the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) for hanging firm and giving us a Budget which continues the tendency, gentle as it is, toward coping with the business of spending money as opposed to the idea of getting more employers out working and providing jobs. It is a slow route, but we have taken the first step in a long journey. I hope the people of Canada understand that. That is more important than all the childish prattle we hear about the per centage of employed and unemployed. The mere fact that there is unemployment is enough of a challenge.
Let me turn to interest rates, a subject that I am sure Members will understand is very dear to me. During the 1984
election campaign we pledged to bring down interest rates. That was the first priority of all the promises we made. This was addressed in the statement of November, 1984 and dealt with again in the 1985 Budget. Slowly, interest rates are beginning to stabilize, but I can still think of five major areas that need to be addressed. However, the fact is that interest rates have declined by some three points.
I will not be satisfied until interest rates are at their proper level. At best, the interest rate should be at 3 per cent, but that will never happen because of the inflationary factor.
All western countries have been guided by a group of experts who believe in the doctrine that all one's faith should be put in a single theory such as the spending theory of Keynes or the monetarist theory.
While there is truth in those theories, one should re-evaluate the progress of such a theory if it collapses. I hear Members from all Parties in the House call for expenditures on various items. While it is necessary to make some expenditures, we should remember that we can only make progress if we have a solid platform on which to proceed.
Let me give some examples. During the last 40 years, and particularly the last 20 years, we have been told that the way to stop inflation is to raise interest rates. That theory was forced on the Government when I was a Minister in 1958. Now I am in all the books as having been the stupid one who fought Coyne. However, 25 years later, the facts are out. We were told that interest rates should be kept high in order to stop consumers from buying too much, and that higher interest rates would maintain the dollar at a higher level.
Let us consider what has happened in the last two months. The United States, Canada and Europe have been dealing with interest rates, and when they declined, the dollar went up to 75 cents and is holding. How can those who preached that doctrine for 40 years continue to do so?
A committee of the House met on this subject in 1979. We asked the Governor of the Bank of Canada for the evidence behind his claim that interest rates must be raised to keep inflation down. He said that he did not have evidence but just believed it was the proper action because all the experts supported that. We asked for evidence to show that high interest rates would keep the dollar up, since it was declining during the entire time interest rates were being raised. As I said, in the last two months interest rates have gone down and the dollar has risen.
All of the charts, going back to the Dana-Porter report of 1961, I believe, show the same truth. However, when will the experts in the Department of Finance and the Bank of Canada read the charts and figures and see the reality?
We must face our responsibility, collect the evidence, of which there has been much in the last two months, and proceed on the basis of that evidence. We do not know any better theory; we only know what we see and that we should not proceed on the basis of something that does not work. We
February 20, 1987

should let common sense prevail while we attempt to make the country run better.
I do not believe there is a complete answer to this question, nor does anyone pretend that there is. The economists confessed 30 years ago that they did not know where they were nor where they were going, but they still make a living and make the same predictions today. I have met most economists over the years and have had full and formal discussions with them.
While we all enjoy partisan discussions across the floor of the House of Commons, I believe the one thing we must have in common is the realization that none of us know the final answer. We should encourage the Government to keep moving forward slowly with small improvements in the hope that the economy will improve. If we attempt to correct the situation in a rush, by pouring money in to solve the problem, we will be faced with the same dilemma that the Keynesian conclusions forced upon Canada.
In 1985, an article in the local paper contained a headline, which perhaps would not have enticed many readers. However, it is very true. The headline reads: "Presto! The new economic molecule". In this article, in which the author talks about economists and the economy, he made the following conclusion:
Rigid orthodoxy is absolutely dead.
This is the final point I wish to leave with the House. We will all be dead if we only worship single doctrines. We cannot conduct our affairs by making rigid guidelines. With our rapidly increasing knowledge, it is not correct to place politics over facts. We must peer into the mist and try to move steadily toward a sensible goal. While there are many other problems, the interest rate problem is the greatest because it affects everything else. The theory about the molecule in this article is a reflection of what is happening.
Since there are many factors which affect these indicators, those who follow one doctrine will not succeed. While it is sometimes difficult to accept, it is much better to make slow and steady progress than to rush backward and forward.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for
Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) has many years of experience in the House. I want to seek his wisdom on this question of corporation tax. There are some who feel that corporation taxes should be increased dramatically because corporations are not paying their fair share. On the other hand, there are those who say that corporate taxes are essentially regressive because they are passed straight on to the consumer. Will he share his wisdom on this question of corporate tax?

Mr. Speaker, I answered that question in general in my speech. When talking about corporations, politicians are simply using that title as a buzz word. We are working together to better appreciate corporations.
The Budget-Mr. Hamilton
The corporation today, politically, is the flogging horse, but as one thinks through it, one finds that whether the corporation is large or small, whether it is a farmer or a householder, one has to have money before one can pay taxes. In other words, we have to have profit. And if we have to have profit, then we had better make certain that our tax level will allow us to make a profit. That is why the tax reforms in the United States which were announced a year ago, and the tax reforms I expect will be announced here, will show, I am sure, a rich decline for corporations, applying to all levels. I predict, from the experience of the Kennedy reductions and the Reagan reductions, and others I could mention, that if we can get the rate of taxes down, the amount of money will increase. Therefore, we should quit thinking of the corporation as a bogeyman that we have to clobber politically. We must think of a way of how to get that horse working. The only thing corporations have been able to do this last 20 or 30 years is to go into mergers to take advantage of the tax law, not producing any new goods at all. However, whether the corporation is large or small is not the point. The fact is that we have to give the producer some form of profit on his labour and work.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank the Hon. Member for certainly one of the best speeches I have heard during this budget debate. He gave us a special type of perspective, and I want to thank him for that. It sure beats the hollow, rancorous kind of comments coming from the other side of this House, not just from the Liberal Party but from the New Democratic Party as well. I sometimes wonder if those Hon. Members have been on another planet during this last decade.
I would like to ask the Minister to comment on a couple of things. I do want to underscore how correct he was in stressing the importance of interest rates. I agree with the Hon. Member that if I could single out one factor which needed to be highlighted as far as getting our economy going again is concerned, it would have to be interest rates. That was done by this Government through a few different steps. We had to dismantle the national energy policy, which was a tragedy for the oil industry. FIRA was another negative approach as far as new investments were concerned. That has been replaced, not just in name but in the approach that we certainly welcome investment into this country. I think it was touched on earlier today that most Canadians would welcome the Budget of the Hon. Member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) of 1979 in which we had a relatively minor increase in gasoline tax. But thanks to the coalition on the other side, Canadians were plunged into another four years of record-setting deficits. Thanks to this particular Government and thanks to the leadership of the Hon. Member for Etobicoke Centre (Mr. Wilson) we have finally turned the corner.
My specific question concerns the Hon. Member's theory on deficits. No country can go on forever without having some deficits. What does the Hon. Member think about the fact that
The Budget-Mr. Hamilton
under the Liberal Government a record was set of 11 successive years of deficits? I think there might have been at least one or two good economic years in that period. Should the Liberal Government have been setting those deficits even in good times?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The Hon. Member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) has only one minute left for a succinct answer.

1 can answer in one sentence. The answer is no. The deficit is simply a measuring device on how much one is behind at a particular time. It is not dangerous in itself but the accumulation of those things eventually ruin you.
